articles.title: Pinehurst Station Opens September 30
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: Today Sound Transit announced Pinehurst station will open September 30, 2026. Located between Shoreline South and Northgate stations, Pinehurst is the first ever Link infill station. The area around the station has been slow to develop as it is primarily occupied by Jackson Park Golf Course and I-5. The new King County Metro Route 77 stops next to Pinehurst station and provides east/west service along N 130th St and NE 125th St.
Pinehurst station was approved as part of ST3 in 2016 and was accelerated to open 5 years before its original projected opening in 2031.
Trains on the 1 Line and 2 Line will begin serving Pinehurst station at 5am on September 30 and a community celebration will take place later in the day.

articles.title: Sammamish and Renton Bus Trip
articles.author: Mike Orr
paras: This article is brought to you by the numbers 269 and 111. Those were the first routes I wanted to try in the August 29th service change last Saturday. I’d never seen Sammamish except once or twice in a car because it had little bus access, and I’d never been to northeast Renton. So on the first day of the new service I did a bus trip to both those areas. This article is a long ramble about that trip, with route times and ridership and neighborhood observations along the way. It begins after the fold.
3:02 – 3:16 pm. (14 minutes.) 3 minute wait for a route running every 10 minutes. Ridership: Typical.
Since there would be nowhere to get a sandwich at Marymoor Village or South Bellevue stations, I stopped at a hot dog stand at Westlake Park.
3:26 – 3:41. (14 minutes.) Wait is complicated because I didn’t intend to take this route. Ridership: I was the only passenger.

I’d intended to take the 269, but the eastbound bus bay at Mercer Island station had no sign telling which routes stopped there. The next-arrival display just said “269: [in 50 minutes]” but didn’t say which direction. So I didn’t know if this was the right stop, or which other routes stopped here. This 269 is supposed to run every 30 minutes, so if the display was accurate the next run wouldn’t show up. The other bus bay is across the street, and a 215 was laying over at it. So I crossed the street to the other bay. It had a routes sign but it was out of date (before the service change). The 215 started moving, so I crossed the street back to the first stop. I wondered if the 215 would stop there, how it would make a U-turn to get to it (it must have used the new roundabout), whether I could reach it before it passed, and whether I wanted to take it. I was hoping for the full 269 experience from Mercer Island through Sammamish to Marymoor Village. But if I couldn’t take the 269 today, the 215 would at least take me to Issaquah Highlands P&R, which was one of my goals.
At the bus stop a would-be passenger asked, “Do you go to North Bend?” The driver explained it wasn’t one of the North Bend 215 runs.
4:00 – 4:42. (42 minutes.) 15 minute wait for a 30 minute route. So it was on time and the display had been wrong.

Ridership: None from Mercer Island. 3 on at Issaquah Highlands P&R. 1 on/1 off at South Sammamish P&R. 2 off at SE 20th. 1 off at SE 16th with e-scooter. 1 on at NE 4th, 1 on at NE 8th. 1 on at Bear Creek P&R. One woman almost got in but she was going the other way. 4 off at Marymoor Village station.

The bus stop signs at Issaquah Highlands P&R are also out of date. I got off the 215 and asked the driver where to get the 269 to Sammamish/Marymoor. He pointed and said “Bay 1”. The stop pole had a current 269 schedule, but the number board was out of date. A 269 westbound stopped there. I asked the driver if both directions stop at the same stop, and he said they do.

Sammamish is very suburban: large houses, woods, open space lawns, reservoir ponds, other ponds that may be for flood control, and three shopping centers. It reminded me of growing up in eastern Bellevue in the 1970s and 80s, but with larger houses. The first shopping center was a QFC supermarket plaza. The second had a multistory building with Metropolitan Market, an impressive new urbanist format. The third was the largest, three shopping centers on adjacent blocks, with Safeway.

The Redmond segment has a surprisingly large number of local stops and streets. I always thought of the 269 as a Sammamish route, but it serves the eastern part of Redmond too. It’s all offices there, so it must be to serve those office parks, or to get Sammamish riders to those office parks.

There were more restaurants near Marymoor Station than I’d noticed before, so maybe I could have gotten a sandwich there after all. I have been to Stone there, my favorite Korean restaurant. (There’s one in SLU too.)
At Marymoor station I saw a routes schedule that had the 547 night ride, half hourly between midnight and 5am.

I went into Marymoor Park to find a restroom before the second phase of my journey. It’s a 10 minute walk from the station entrance around the Velodrome. On the way is a children’s play area with a child-sized locomotive train kids can sit in. One kiddo there said “Hoo hoo” like a train whistle.

I then went up to the top of the P&R to see the 6th floor view I’d heard about. I’d been wanting to do that ever since the Starter Line opened. I imagined an expansive view overlooking downtown Redmond and Marymoor Park. It wasn’t. I could barely glimpse two buildings in downtown Redmond through the trees. I couldn’t see much of Marymoor Park beyond the Velodrome.
5:21 – 5:42. (21 minutes.) 2 minute wait for a 10 minute route. Ridership: Typical.
6:00 – 6:30. (30 minutes.) 16 minute wait for a 30 minute route.
Ridership: 8 on at South Bellevue station. 3 off at Newport Hills P&R. 1 off at 44th (Kennydale), 1 on with bike. 6 on/offs in the Renton Highlands. The last run was at 7:30pm.

The route signs and schedules at South Bellevue station were current. The new schedule signs show all the streets the routes serve, instead of just the upcoming streets for this direction. I like the old way better. It’s disorienting when the first entry is way behind you.
The 111, 547, and 556 all stop at the ex-550 stop. So the express routes are at this stop, and the local routes at the other stop.

The Renton Highlands has a wide variety of 1950s houses, normal-sized houses, and McMansions all next to each other. The front yards are small but not tiny. It feels like a more walkable area than Sammamish. There’s a village with 5 large apartment buildings, a library, and Safeway. And another large building saying “Renton Housing Authority” for low-income housing.

I was debating whether to go to the end of the route and wait for a return bus to the Highlands, or to get off at NE 4th & Union which I guessed might be the center of the Highlands. But there was only two more hours of daylight so I got off as soon as it reached NE 4th, where the 111 and 105 cross. That’s at Renton Technical College. (So that’s where the college is.) Food options were limited to McDonald’s or a gas station mini-mart, so I was glad I’d already had a hot dog.

I just missed a 105 which passed as I was walking to the transfer stop. The next one wouldn’t be for a half hour. So I started walking. I guessed a 30 minute walk would get me at least halfway to downtown Renton, but I didn’t really know because I’d only been to the Renton Highlands once, and not to this part.

The reason I walked was there were more interesting things to look at along the way than in Sammamish and Issaquah, it was downhill, and it has a full-sized sidewalk. NE 4th Street quickly turned into NE 3rd Street, and that continued down the hill and under 405 to Sunset Blvd and Houser Way.

At the 30 minute mark I reached downtown Renton and the next 105 passed me. It took another 20 minutes to reach Renton Transit Center. But I don’t mind walking in downtown Renton: it’s a walkable downtown, I got to go through Liberty Park and the library bridge over the Cedar River, and I discovered several more blocks of historic retail buildings than I realized were there.
All the 105s I saw had a yellow stripe on top and were electric buses. I also saw a RapidRide F that was half purple and an electric bus.
7:30 – 8:00. (30 minutes.) 6 minute wait for a 15 minute route.

Ridership: 9 at Renton TC. 1 on in downtown Renton. 3 off in western Renton. 2 off in Skyway. 1 on in far south Seattle. 3 on/1 off at the Rainier Beach Safeway. 2 off/1 on at Henderson & Renton Ave. 1 off/1 on at Rainier Beach station. 12 people remained on the bus as it continued.
8:11 – 8:41. (30 minutes.) 9 minute wait for a 10 minute route. Ridership: Standing room only. 7 on at Rainier Beach (or more if I missed anybody at the northern doors).

articles.title: Seattle Parks shaping new rules for Denny Blaine nude beach
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Seattle Parks and Recreation is opening public review on proposed Supplemental Use Guidelines for Denny Blaine Park following a recent court decision shaping the public shoreline at the historically recognized LGBTQ+ nude beach.
The community group formed to protect Denny Blaine says now is the time “for the people who actually use and love this park to make their voices heard.”

The public process includes a community meeting on Tuesday, September 15th at 6 PM at the Miller Community Center , located at 330 19th Ave E. Seattle Parks representatives will gather community feedback during the session before the guidelines are finalized.
A virtual public meeting will follow on September 17 at 6 PM and an online feedback period will remain open through October 5 to capture written public input.

While specific park configurations remain constrained by the court’s ruling, advocacy organization Friends of Denny Blaine say they have met with city officials to help ensure park users shape the final policy. Priority areas targeted for public input include improving physical accessibility, installing screening to protect visitors’ privacy from unwanted surveillance, and adding thoughtful landscaping, signage, and amenities. Community advocates are also urging the city to officially recognize Denny Blaine’s history as a queer and clothing-optional gathering place.
The guidelines also must comply to the court’s rulings, the city says:

Several aspects of the proposed guidelines are set by court order and cannot be unilaterally changed by the City through the rulemaking process. These include the designation of clothing-optional and clothing-required areas, the specific line where the areas are divided, the requirement for visual screening between the areas, the allowance of toplessness throughout the park, and the minimum frequency of visits and monitoring by Park Rangers and maintenance staff.
The city says the court has “also required SPR to install some additional screening to ensure that clothing-optional areas of the park are not visible from neighboring properties.”
CHS reported here in July as a judge denied a bid by a group of neighbors and nearby property owners to close the park over complaints of public nudity, sexual activity, and disorder.

In his decision, Judge Samuel Chung sided with the City of Seattle and Friends of Denny Blaine in keeping the two-acre park on the shores of Lake Washington open — and nude — calling Denny Blaine “a limited natural resource that must be shared by the residents of the neighborhood and the Park’s visitors.”

The decision came with caveats after several findings that the court said justified the neighbors’ claims around lewd acts and criminal activity at the park. In the ruling, the judge said the city must implement and manage a previously approved abatement plan, and “develop and implement a park specific user plan and code of conduct to address overcrowding, safety, and prohibited and acceptable behaviors.”
The new guideline review runs parallel to broader community sessions starting late September regarding long-term park investments and improvements:
Provide feedback on the proposed Supplemental Use Guidelines :

Neighbors are also watching how a major area real estate listing will play out. A 1928-era, 5,500-square-foot mansion neighboring the park hit the market this summer for $4.65 million, a 66% premium to the last time it sold in 2015.

“Tucked into the heart of Denny Blaine and only steps from the shores of Lake Washington, this stunning Mediterranean estate is a rare offering, where timeless European charm meets refined Northwest living,” the listing reads.

articles.title: Coffee TAB Central District ready to open at 23rd and Jackson
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: A key neighborhood hangout is going back in motion in the Central District as Coffee TAB is ready to open at 23rd and Jackson.

“We’re intentional about everything, from the way we pull a shot to the neighborhoods we choose to serve. We want to breathe new life into places by building something that serves the community well—somewhere people gather, form relationships, and feel a sense of belonging,” founder Jonathan Tran said in the joint announcement from TAB and Vulcan Real Estate , the owner of the building and the surrounding shopping center. “Opening at 23rd & Jackson is another chance to live that out. It’s about investing in a neighborhood, creating jobs, expanding opportunities for young adults, and becoming part of the fabric of the Central Area.”

In addition to restoring much missed coffee service at the corner, the opening of Coffee TAB CD is an important milestone after years of concerns around public safety and street disorder in the area as the building sat empty.

In July, CHS was the first to report on the plans for Coffee TAB to fill the space, the third cafe for the four-year-old nonprofit dedicated to espresso and jobs training. The corner has been a sore spot. After Starbucks pulled out over what it said were concerns about public safety, Vulcan, the City of Seattle , and Black Coffee Northwest planned to open a new cafe in the space in a plan backed by Mayor Bruce Harrell’s office, and District 3 representative Joy Hollingsworth that ultimately fell apart despite announced intentions of rebuilding Black ownership in the neighborhood.

Hollingsworth marked progress at the corner in a recent video celebrating Coffee TAB’s opening , saying she is “super excited for this corner to activate” and is looking forward to a new community gathering space.
Appearing with Hollingsworth and Tran, State Sen. Rebecca Saldaña summed up the excitement.

“Because 23rd and Jackson is the heart of the Central District. It’s the heart of our community, and this place has been empty for way too long,” Saldaña says. “Our young people and our elders need a place to hang out, and the coffee is really delicious.”

Meanwhile, larger economic and community challenges remain with the shuttered buildings left by the closure of the center’s Walgreens and the shutdown of the neighborhood’s Amazon Fresh grocery store across the street.
Coffee Tab will be celebrating the new space in October as it holds a silent auction and fundraiser supporting its Barista Apprenticeship Program at the Jackson location.
Final inspections were needed before the space could finally reopen, according to a recent social media update.
Coffee TAB is ready to open at 2300 S Jackson. Learn more at coffeetab.org .

articles.title: Seattle's Pinehurst Light Rail Station Will Open September 30
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: As of today, Pinehurst Station officially has an opening date: Wednesday, September 30. The infill light rail station between Northgate and South Shoreline will serve both the 1 Line and the 2 Line, attracting an estimated 3,400 daily boardings. The late September opening coincides with the start of classes at the University of Washington and meets the agency's goal of opening the station in the third quarter of the year.

The combined headways of the two lines gives riders frequent service between Lynnwood and the International District, with trains arriving every four to five minutes. Sound Transit has pledged to keep riders abreast of opening festivities on its Pinehurst website , but there are signs that the event will be a subdued affair compared to other recent line openings.

This summer, Sound Transit crews have been hard at work putting finishing touches on the elevated station, which sits just north of NE 130th Street. The platform sits high up overlooking I-5 and leafy neighborhoods and parks surrounding it.

Among those finishing touches is station art, which was designed by Seattle-based artist Romson Bustillo , who was born on the island of Mindanao in the Philippines. The art will have a South Pacific feel, with human and animal figures brightly patterned in red, yellow, and green.

"[Bustillo's] layered works and immersive collaborations go back to his Philippine lineage, his South Seattle/Pacific Northwest upbringing, and numerous research travels," Sound Transit's Katie Metzger noted in 2025 . "His artwork will be translated into richly colored, porcelain enamel panels that wrap around the entrances and into both north and south lobbies."

Adding a station to this location has been long in the making, a project approved in 2016's Sound Transit 3 (ST3) ballot measure, grafting a stop onto ST2's Lynnwood Link Extension. In 2020, Sound Transit accelerated the project's timeline from 2031 to 2025, which was later revised to 2026, to put it closer to Lynnwood Link's 2024 launch. That occurred largely due to the advocacy of District 5 Councilmember Debora Juarez, who served on the Sound Transit board at the time and had lobbied to get the station included in the ST3 plan in the first place.

Like most ST3 expansions, the station faced the threat of major delay, but survived the 2021 realignment still on its accelerated course in part because adding an infill station years later only adds expense and complication. The construction work next to an active rail line was complicated enough happening in the immediate aftermath, requiring some single tracking during platform work.

"These decisions ultimately resulted in a faster, less disruptive construction process for the station to be able to open ahead of its original schedule," Constantine said Thursday. "I would also note that September 30th is the first day of classes for fall quarter at the University of Washington. So we will be welcoming aboard students, faculty, and staff who have now a more convenient way to get to campus."

Thanks to a funded plan for the infill station, the initial build of Lynnwood Link was able to incorporate space for the Pinehurst platform into the elevated structure. More recently, workers came back to fill out with station amenities, like elevators, escalators, and stairs down to street level, where card readers, signage, bike parking, and a new drop-off zone for paratransit vehicles welcome riders.

King County Metro has already added a Route 77 in the fall service change that will feed the station when it opens, connecting Lake City and Bitter Lake like never before. Before the change, the station location was a dead zone for bus service, but the case for the station always rested in part on adding an east-west bus line to serve a broader corridor, like the 77 will do, using NE 130th and 125th Streets.

“Traveling around our city and region should be easy and affordable. Every new light rail station gets us further toward that goal. Pinehurst Station will create more and better options for people in North Seattle to get to the important places in their lives,” said Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson said in a statement. "It’s great news that people now have a date to look forward to and plan around. Next stop - Pinehurst Station!”

The Seattle delegation on the Sound Transit Board of Directors argued keeping the Pinehurst opening on track was a priority and an early win deliverable for the ST3 measure, and they were backed by a campaign from local residents . Seattle officials promised rezones nearby to grow a dense neighborhood in the midst of the freeway-adjacent station. However, those rezones hit the Seattle process and have only been partially delivered so far.

Seattle attached the long-studied Pinehurst rezones to the Comprehensive Plan major update that was due in 2024, but delayed by the Harrell Administration before being mired in citizen appeals . As a result, the City has failed to have its new zoning plan in place by the time the station open. In turn, this means no large-scale housing development projects are under construction in the vicinity.

The draft zoning plan includes a relative small patch of Neighborhood Commercial 85-foot zoning near the station, and some broader patches of Midrise zoning, before giving way to Lowrise. When the upzones do go live, eight-story apartment buildings with some ground-floor retail could be on the way. Just how quickly is uncertain, with the City appearing to have missed the development cycle by dragging its feet. Housing permit activity have been trending sharply downward across Seattle.
Even in 2023, the Pinehurst rezone delays drew the ire of Dave Baker, the former Kenmore City Councilmember who served on the Sound Transit board of the time.

“I’m sorry Mayor Harrell, I’m not trying to throw stones, but it’s just reality that they’ve had the opportunity to increase zoning in the area to make it more transit-friendly, but it’s still not done,” Baker said. “They’ve had since 2015 to fix the zoning, and it’s now 2023 and the zoning has still not been fixed. I would love to see a successful station… and the system to be as functional as it can. Everything else seems to be happening except this one.”
Harrell brushed off the criticism, declining to respond at the time.

Seattle's planning efforts have also punted on the issue of Jackson Park, a fenced-off, 160-acre, publicly-owned 27-hole golf course which advocates had called for adapting to broader, more accessible park uses. Some also called for integrating housing into the campus , which likely would require a park land swap given Initiative 42 stipulations, which prohibits park lands from being appropriated for other uses without making up for the loss of land elsewhere.
As it stands, the golf course disrupts walking routes to the station from the northeast, in addition to putting a low-density use next to high-capacity transit.

While Pinehurst has an imminent opening date, things are less certain for ST3-approved infill stations at Graham Street in South Seattle and at Boeing Access Road in Tukwila. Both stations were formerly promised in 2031, but Tukwila has no opening date after the board's May 28 vote left the agency without the full amount for construction included in its financial plan.

Meanwhile, Graham Street was only saved from the chopping block when the City of Seattle gave assurances of up to $30 million in last-in funding to back the project. That could prove to be a tricky precedent for the City to have set down the road, as the agency grapples with more overruns on Seattle projects. But riders can take solace in Graham Street remaining on course to open in 2031 or thereabouts.

“The opening of Pinehurst Station is a significant milestone as the first infill station added to an existing light rail line. It’s another step forward in delivering the light rail investments communities across King County have been counting on,” said King County Executive Girmay Zahilay in a statement. "I look forward to continued progress on the remaining infill stations, including Graham Street Station and Boeing Access Road Station.”

Constantine pledged that the lessons learned from Pinehurst will inform plans for Graham Street and Tukwila's infill station, which faces stiff headwinds due to ballooning cost estimates. While Pinehurst Station came in at $240 million, estimates for Boeing Access Road have jump as high as $475 million .

articles.title: After Voters Pass Connect Tacoma Levy, Officials Eye Next Steps
articles.author: Carolyn Bick
paras: The passage of the Connect Tacoma: Safe Streets and Sidewalks levy marked a sea change in voter attitude. Just last April, a more ambitious transportation measure failed at the ballot box. But this year, the levy garnered nearly 60% of the vote in the August primary.

“A big lesson that the city learned between last year's failure and this year's success was not taking our community for granted and making sure to start the conversation significantly earlier with more people,” Tacoma Mayor Anders Ibsen said. “The other difference was the content. We listened to the people after last year's failure and we learned that the voters wanted something a bit more modest.”
While the failed 2025 renewal effort included no sunset clause and would have raised funding indefinitely, the 2026 measure includes a 10-year sunset.

The levy serves as a continuation of the 2015 Tacoma Streets Initiative that ended last year. The 2015 initiative, a 10-year funding measure, approved $325 million for repair and maintenance around the city, including in residential neighborhoods. The Connect Tacoma levy, which goes into effect on Jan. 1, 2027, raises $200 million over 10 years, and aims to leverage an additional $120 million through grants, investing in transportation projects that address safety, connectivity, and access issues around the city.

But this new levy also comes with several important differences, particularly when it comes to flexibility in what it can fund and the City’s decision to prioritize funding only after allowing residents to weigh in on what upgrades they would like to see. In other words, project lists are still being crafted.

Funding for the 2026 levy comes from a variety of sources, but the bulk of the money — about $200 million of the estimated total — will come from a mix of utility and property taxes. But because these taxes are a continuation of the initiative voters approved in 2015, it means that there’s no actual increase, said Laura Svancarek, the executive director of Tacoma On The Go .

As a local nonprofit organization working towards a safer, more connected Tacoma by providing and advocating for mobility resources, Tacoma On The Go pushed for the levy’s passage and worked with the city on voter outreach, and Svancarek set up a community levy committee. During levy outreach work, one of the biggest concerns the organization heard from voters was that the levy would increase their taxes. With President Donald Trump’s and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s war in Iran continuing to drive up the price of gas and groceries , voters appeared sensitive to the risk of facing further financial hardship.

“Because the renewal did not pass last year, that meant that the original levy expired at the end of 2025. So, technically speaking, this is an increase because those property taxes [temporarily] went away, and now they're coming back,” Svancarek said. “But … they are at the same rate as the previous initial streets levy. Being able to help communicate that to people was pretty significant because it's on the ballot as an increase, but it's not really an increase.”

Like the previous levy, residents will see a tax of $0.20 for every $1,000 of assessed property value, and a 1.5% earnings tax on natural gas, electric, and phone utilities. There are still exemptions for elders and people with disabilities who qualify for property tax relief programs.

The remaining $120 million will come from a mix of grant funding and partnerships. The grant funding, Svancarek said, is “the real superpower of this levy,” and the levy allows the city to leverage more grant match dollars for significant safety work on major arterials, such as South Tacoma Way.

The new levy is broader in what kinds of projects it can fund. While the 2015 initiative’s wording framed funding around streets and transportation infrastructure, the new levy’s wording includes funding for maintenance work, greenways, multimodal transit, and accessibility measures.
The projects the Connect Tacoma levy will fund fall into three categories: Better Neighborhood Streets, Safer Streets for Everyone, and Improved Connections.

The city estimates that about $85 million will go towards the first category, which includes residential street maintenance and improvement, and that about $159 million will go towards the second category of projects, which includes major safety and connectivity overhauls in the city’s busiest corridors and arterials. The city estimates it will allocate the remaining $76 million to the third category of projects, all of which fall under the connectivity umbrella: Americans with Disability Act (ADA) accessibility, trails and greenways, multimodal connections, and more.

But just because the city has roughly budgeted for these different categories doesn’t mean it has a priority list of projects in mind. Wrapped up in all of this work is the question of equity, especially because several areas of the city — such as Hilltop, Fern Hill, and the South End — suffered decades of redlining and neglect.

“While those covenants are gone now, we still live with the repercussions of those policies, and the decades and decades of intentional choices to not invest in neighborhoods that are primarily people of color or low-income families,” Svancarek said. These neighborhoods “face a real infrastructure deficit that the city is now working to address. [ … ] The way [this levy is] structured allows for a lot more flexibility and being able to go into those neighborhoods and fix some of those missing link pieces, finish some of those active transportation connections and be more able to address emerging safety issues than the previous levy allowed. The previous levy was very strict in what it could be used for.”

In 2018, the city developed the Equity Index , which is meant to help address and resolve disparities. The index wasn’t in place when the first levy passed, but the city used it in its outreach work, and will continue to utilize it in developing the projects the levy will fund.

While the city will not choose to, for instance, pave a street purely on equity data without considering other factors, like crashes and pavement condition, Ibsen said, the fact that “you can look at certain neighborhoods and guess where you are based on whether or not a neighborhood has sidewalks or trees [is] not a good thing.”

“You can fairly guess where you are on the basis of 'Does it have sidewalks? Does it have a curb and gutter? Does it have street trees?' [ … ] There is a 10 to 15 degree difference during heat waves in the North End versus the South End,” he said. “To not consider equity would be a grave disservice to our city. Over half of us live south of 6th Avenue, so it absolutely has to be a factor.”

The City said it does not intend to ignore Tacoma’s most dangerous streets, which leaders and staff say are well identified in traffic data. While it’s not among the most dangerous cities in the state for pedestrians and bicyclists, Tacoma continues to have a high fatal crash rate. Last year, 118 pedestrians were involved in crashes. Most of these people were injured, and three of them died. In 2024, 15 pedestrians died in crashes.

In addition to its Equity Index, the City will also be utilizing its six-year Comprehensive Transportation Program and its 20-year Transportation and Mobility Plan , pointing to a need to address the maintenance backlog and get “the most bang for our buck.”
“There is an order of magnitude of cost to rebuilding a completely failed street versus taking a street that's in the middle of its life and adding more life to it,” Ibsen said.

In passing the 2015 levy, voters told the city that they largely wanted the city to focus on residential streets. But based on voter feedback, that is not necessarily true this time around, and assuming that voter accountability stops at the ballot box would be a mistake, explained Public Works Director Ramiro Chavez.

Within the context of resident choice, Chavez explained, the City is in the process of developing a work plan based around the three categories the city designated for levy funding allocation. Staff will present a plan to Tacoma’s Infrastructure, Planning, and Sustainability Committee for feedback around mid-to-late October. He said that he hopes the City will be able to start incorporating specific projects in the late autumn, but also noted that some of those projects may not fit neatly into a 10-year plan, due to the possibility that certain projects’ conditions — particularly when it comes to finances — could change in that time.

“Much of those transportation dollars [do] not directly come from the City. [They come] from the federal and state governments in the form of grant money,” Ibsen explained. “If we had a fixed amount of projects that we said [are] immovable, we can't change anything in 10 years, then that would not only make us incredibly inflexible for opportunities that may come up, but it would deny the community to have any real voice [versus] if we are nimble and we focus our dollars on having great designs at the ready so that our engineers can immediately take advantage of grant opportunities.”

The City also included a program within the levy aimed at accessibility and connectivity fixes, which specifically focuses on ADA improvements, Tacoma’s Safe Routes to School program , sidewalk repairs, and enhancements for people who choose or who have no choice but to get around without a car by walking, rolling, biking, or taking public transit.

In 2017, in partnership with area schools and community organizations, the City launched its Safe Routes to School program. Chavez said that, at this point, Tacoma doesn’t have any locations picked out — “we need to take a little more time as to how we coordinate with the school district, the specific schools, and start identifying what are the specific needs or the gaps” — but that the passage of the levy allows the City to pursue grant opportunities that require local matching dollars. Those matching dollars will come from the levy.

Tacoma is also in the middle of finalizing what is known as its “transition plan,” which is an assessment of all ADA accessibility needs across the city, such as where the city might need to install ADA-compliant ramps or street curbs.

“It may be [that there are] already some existing ramps in the city, as we have all over the place. But [ … ] some of those ramps maybe were built to old standards, maybe 15, 20 years ago, and [by] today's standards [don’t] meet the ADA requirements,” Chavez said. Every new project will also have to be ADA-compliant. Chavez said that the City hopes to finalize that plan early next year.

The city is also using the levy to pursue its tree canopy cover goals , which target 30% tree canopy cover by 2030 — the ratio is around 20% as it stands. While funding for tree cover isn’t directly addressed as part of the overview of any of the three categories, Chavez said that tree cover is actually part and parcel of a safe street or sidewalk. For one, trees provide shade and shelter — and, as Ibsen noted, some places in the city can be 10-15 degrees hotter than others. Trees can also create a more welcoming environment for pedestrians.
But this doesn’t mean the city can just plunk a tree down anywhere in Tacoma and call it a day.

“We have to make sure that we put the right trees at the right location. Over time, trees have been planted across the city, and some instances may not necessarily be the right kind of trees, because they have an effect on the sidewalks,” Chavez said. “Those trees that we may plant may serve a stormwater component, depending on the solutions for the stormwater. [ … ] It's creating that inviting environment, where [ … ] we need the intent of traffic circulation, but also the pedestrians and bicyclists are part of that.”
Chavez also noted that the City is looking into de-paving some areas, and just received a grant from the Department of Ecology to depave some of the medians along S Union Avenue.

“What we're going to be doing in depaving is taking the asphalt or the concrete out and then we'll start planting trees,” he said. “So that is another strategy that we're going to be contemplating down the road because Tacoma is a built environment and there are a lot of paved areas. We're going to have to see what areas [would] be conducive to depave and replant trees in those areas.”
Ibsen said that one of the highlights of the levy is that it gives leaders both “a measurable time frame” and “enough flexibility to chase after grant dollars.”

“This is dedicated money that we will always have lockboxed away towards transportation, which allows our engineers to very strategically focus on having great designs ready to go,” he continued, “and that means that when we apply for grant dollars, which most capital projects, like major resurfacing, major arterials, major connections, [are] going to have to involve [ … ] we have a huge leg up over a lot of the competition [for those grants] because we've already paid for those designs with local dollars.”
But the source of these funds isn’t going to be available forever, given the levy’s 10-year sunset.

“Something I'm endeavoring to do is gathering the same people that we worked with in the initial outreach [ … ] and having some sort of permanent brain trust of these smart people who have a direct stake in the success of this, and making sure that we're permanently baking in their recommendations, their oversight, into how we're spending the money,” Ibsen said.

The mayor also highlighted that he wants the City to keep working on how it prioritizes projects, and how it can encourage housing development in key neighborhoods and continue to build connections and mobility in industrial centers and certain downtown areas “that can really use a shot on the arm, like around [the University of Washington] - Tacoma.”

Most importantly, Ibsen said, the city’s future plans, as he sees them, “have a lot less to do with asking for money and a lot more to do with continuous engagement. That's one of my chief ambitions with this measure [ … ] that we're making engagement the norm rather than just something that we do on a 10-year basis.”

articles.title: Why Seattle waste drivers aren’t getting pricked like sanitation workers in New York (but you should still dispose of your needles in a safer way)
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Automated garbage can lifts mostly protect Seattle collection drivers as the city’s garbage and recycling systems deal with an increase in consumer hypodermic needle use.

Seattle Public Utilities tells CHS it has not recorded an increase in needlestick injuries among contractors servicing the city. Unlike cities where crews manually lift trash bags, Seattle’s residential routes use mechanical arms to empty curbside carts directly into trucks, keeping drivers away from thin bags and protruding needles.

Cities with manual collection face different hazards. In New York City, where Department of Sanitation crews lift bags by hand, the agency has logged 49 needlestick injuries through early August. That surpassed the 46 incidents reported in 2025 and rose from 18 in 2020. The increase led New York to raise fines for improper needle disposal from $100 to $250. DSNY does not test recovered needles, but officials attribute the rise to more residents using at-home injectable drugs.

Manual collection remains standard in older, denser East Coast cities where narrow streets and row homes prevent automated side-loader trucks from operating. In Philadelphia, the city’s Community Life Improvement Program and Department of Sanitation deploy specialized teams equipped with puncture-resistant gear to clear corridors like Kensington, where union representatives with AFSCME District Council 33 have cited worker safety and punctures from loose needles during manual trash collection. In Boston, where contracted haulers physically toss bags into rear compactors, city public health officials conduct targeted daily needle sweeps along high-traffic corridors like the “Mass and Cass” area to clear loose syringes before curbside collection begins.

The municipal strain follows a broader shift documented by The New York Times , which reported last month that syringes and auto-injectors have migrated from clinical settings directly onto domestic bathroom vanities. According to the report, nearly one in five U.S. adults has tried an injectable GLP-1 medication like Ozempic, while consumer interest in injectable peptides and at-home fertility treatments like IVF — which grew nearly 40% between 2018 and 2026 — has routinely pushed medical sharps into households.

That proliferation has created new hazards in our waste The New York Times reports sanitation workers there frequently encounter exposed, loose needles when lifting plastic garbage bags, with one New York City department supervisor telling the paper that crews regularly open bags to find needles completely unshielded. The surge is also hitting retail businesses. The Times cited a Nordstrom Rack restroom that posted signs pleading with shoppers to stop dropping GLP-1 syringes into its public sharps containers due to the escalating fees the retailer pays to empty them.

SPU says that it does not track the source or type of discarded needles, meaning it cannot link box totals to specific drugs like GLP-1 weight-loss medications. While automated trucks protect Seattle drivers, the machinery does not protect downstream workers.

Washington law and King County health rules prohibit sharps in household garbage or curbside recycling. SPU directs residents to use puncture-resistant containers and drop them at public boxes or the North Transfer Station.

Improperly discarded sharps still reach sorting plants. Industry publications note that because retail pharmacies rarely provide mail-back boxes with injectable prescriptions, people often throw pens into the trash or stash needles in milk jugs and soda bottles sent to recycling.

Compactors inside automated trucks crush those plastic jugs, scattering loose needles into the sorting stream. According to the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, needlestick wounds risk exposure to hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV.

The danger then falls on sorting facilities, where workers manually pull recyclables off conveyor belts. A study by the Environmental Research & Education Foundation and the Solid Waste Association of North America estimated somewhere around 1,000 needlestick injuries happen annually at recycling facilities, with manual sorters injured at a rate of 3.9 per 100 workers. More than half of surveyed facilities report finding loose needles mixed into recyclables daily or weekly.

A few drugmakers and select specialty pharmacies provide free mail-back sharps containers for specific injectables, but standard retail pharmacies rarely include disposal with prescriptions. As a result, safe disposal largely depends on state initiatives — such as Washington’s free prepaid injector mail-back service — and municipal drop-off sites provided by utilities like SPU.

Seattle’s tough years of drug crisis including spikes in intravenous drug use may be helping keep workers safe from the pricks. Seattle Public Utilities maintains 23 public drop boxes across the city for safe disposal. The disposal boxes, located on city property and public rights-of-way such as exterior restroom walls in parks like Cal Anderson , are heavy-duty, tamper-resistant deposit chutes. Residents drop sealed containers into the chute directly at any time.

Seattle’s drop boxes are also busier. SPU reports it collected 446,716 sharps through its 23 public drop boxes through the first half of 2026 — about 22% more than the pace in the previous two years. It’s unknown how many of the rest of those needles are taking a dangerous path to the landfill or recycling plant.
Learn more from King County Public Health on how to safely dispose of needles at home .

articles.title: The Ultimate ORCA Speedrun
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: At 9:59am last Friday, I boarded Everett Transit Route 29 at Everett Transit Mall Station. While the six other passengers on the bus were traveling to work, home, or somewhere else, for me this trip was the first segment of my region-wide ORCA speedrun. Transit speedrunning is the process of visiting every station in a transit system as fast as possible. In cities/regions with complex rail transit networks, such as San Francisco or New York , competitors look for new routes to beat the previous record. While the Link light rail system now has 3 lines across Puget Sound, the speedrun route is fairly straightforward . Our rail network is not complex enough to provide other potential routes that are faster. However, the broader ORCA network is quite complex.

One Regional Card for All (ORCA) powers transit fares for nine transit agencies across four counties in Washington. Visiting every stop in the ORCA network would take months, so the ORCA speedrun has a simpler goal: ride every mode of fixed-route transit offered by each agency in the ORCA pod, as fast as possible. This includes every type bus service, rail service, and ferry service from each of the nine agencies. For example, King County Metro offers three types of bus service: local, express, and RapidRide. Likewise, Kitsap Transit has both Fast Ferries and Foot Ferries. In total, there are 21 different modes across the nine agencies. Paratransit, dial-a-ride-transit, or other on-demand services are not included. City Beautiful and The Transit Bandit have completed similar speedruns using seven of the transit modes in Seattle.

Centered around downtown Seattle, ORCA is supported by agencies to the north, south, and west. For my speedrun, I started in the north (Everett) and planned to finish in the south (Tacoma). I shared updates in real-time on Bluesky and a full map of the run is available here .

Snohomish County has two dedicated transit agencies: Everett Transit (ET) and Community Transit (CT). ET is one of the smaller agencies on the list, it just runs local bus service. CT, meanwhile, has local bus routes, Express bus routes and Swift routes.

My trip on Route 29 checked the Everett Transit box. I got off the bus at the South Everett Freeway Station and transferred to an inbound Community Transit Express Route 905. Route 905 returned to I-5 and traveled directly to Lynnwood Transit Center. As I would need to return back to Lynnwood TC to board Link to get to Seattle, this next segment required an out-and-back using both Swift and a local route. I boarded the next Orange Line bus towards Edmonds College and took it one stop to Hwy 99. Thankfully, the traffic signal at Hwy 99 & 196th St was in my favor so I could catch the Lynnwood-bound Route 166 across the street with seconds to spare.

Link is the best option for traveling between Lynnwood and Seattle. The 40 minute ride was a nice opportunity to relax after a few very close transfers in Snohomish County. In Seattle, I had about an hour to ride five different modes: Metro bus, Metro Express bus, Seattle Streetcar, ST Express bus, and the Seattle Center Monorail. While I had planned most of the day, this hour was improvised. At Westlake station, I got off the 1 Line and walked over to the waiting South Lake Union streetcar. I hopped aboard and we departed a few minutes later. After two stops, I alighted the streetcar at Denny Way and boarded an eastbound Route 8 bus. As we sped down the new bus lane on Denny, I noticed a ST Express Route 577 bus was about to start its trip to Federal Way. I got off Route 8 after just one stop and ran to the bus stop at Boren Ave & Virginia St. The Route 577 bus arrived a few moments later, exactly on time.

I now had just two modes left for downtown Seattle: the Seattle Center Monorail and a Metro Express bus. Most Metro Express buses run during peak hours so my only option was Route 28X. I rode Route 577 a few stops to Stewart St & 7th Ave. After a short walk to Westlake Center Mall, I boarded a well timed monorail train and made my way to Seattle Center. I sat near the front of the train as I needed to make a quick exit to catch the next bus. A southbound Route 28X bus was scheduled to depart from 7th & Thomas at 11:52am, four minutes after the monorail arrived at Seattle Center. A four minute transfer is usually fine, but this bus stop was a 7 minute walk from the monorail station.

After a short jog I made it to the bus stop 2 minutes early (the bus was 1 minute late). I boarded the 28X bus to check off the last mode needed in downtown Seattle. My next scheduled ride was the 12:30pm West Seattle Water Taxi operated by King County Metro. With 25 minutes to spare I decided to ride Metro’s Waterfront Shuttle.

I arrived back at Pier 50 at 12:19 and joined the queue to board my first boat of the day. Metro’s West Seattle Water Taxi took just 10 minutes to reach Seacrest Dock. I boarded on DART Route 773 for a quick ride to Avalon Ave & Bradford, just south of the West Seattle Bridge. After crossing the street, I caught an inbound C Line bus back to downtown Seattle. This RapidRide bus was the fourth and final mode of the day from King County Metro.

The C Line bus sailed across the West Seattle Bridge and dropped me off across the street from the Seattle Ferry Terminal. After enjoying some of the ferry terminal amenities, we (my wife joined me for this section) boarded the Seattle – Bremerton Washington State Ferries route. The hour-long trip sailed by and we arrived in Bremerton at 2:39pm, just 9 minutes behind schedule. Despite the delay we had a few minutes for a delicious lunch at Mezcalitos. At 3:30p, we walked back over to the ferry terminal to catch the smallest boat of the day: a Kitsap Transit Foot Ferry to Annapolis. The Admiral Pete was packed to standing-room-only as we made the short trip to Annapolis. We alighted the vessel with everyone else and started to walk down the surprisingly long dock. When we were halfway to land, the boat’s engines roared to life and it sailed away. This was not the plan. We were supposed to take that same boat back to Bremerton. The 15-minute wait for the next sailing put the most important transfer of the day in jeopardy.

The next boat back to Bremerton was scheduled to get us back to Bremerton at 4:07pm. That would leave just four minutes to catch the 4:11pm Worker/Driver bus from the Puget Sound Naval Shipyard (PSNS). Worker/Driver buses run just once per day in each direction, so missing it would end this speed run attempt. After enjoying a private boat experience on the Foot Ferry trip back to Bremerton, I left the backpack with my wife and sprinted to PSNS. About a minute later, the retractable bollards descended and the Route 613 (Chico) bus rolled through the gate.

Kitsap Transit’s Worker/Driver routes are unique in Puget Sound. They travel from across Kitsap County to downtown Bremerton and PSNS. While they are designed for PSNS employees (and only PSNS employees can ride them within the facility), their one stop outside the PSNS gate makes them available to the public. I did confirm that these routes are open to the public with Kitsap Transit staff a few weeks ago. As the Worker/Driver routes travel long distances, they have far stop spacing. I rode Route 631 one stop (2.5 miles), to Kitsap Way & Marine Dr. Here, I had a lofty 10 minute transfer to Kitsap Route 212 back to the ferry terminal.

As luck would have it, Route 212 was running 17 minutes behind schedule and was scheduled to arrive at the Bremerton Terminal at 4:57pm. I needed to catch the 5:00pm Fast Ferry back to Seattle. As the Fast Ferry requires all passengers to be on board 2 minutes before departure, this would cut it way to close. Fortunately, there was a Route 226 bus from the same stop that was scheduled to arrive at the terminal at 4:55pm. Still too close for comfort, but I didn’t have another option. Route 226 arrived on time and I was finally heading back to the ferry terminal. While on board, I noticed the Route 226 had a slight detour in downtown Bremerton. Still worried about catching the Fast Ferry, I decided to get off the bus at Pacific and MLK Way and run the rest of the way. I met back up with my wife and we joined the line to board the Fast Ferry at 4:56pm.

The Fast Ferry was busy! Nearly every seat was occupied as we made the 30-minute trip back to Seattle. We got off the boat at 5:33pm, leaving just 12 minutes to catch the 5:45pm Sounder train to Tacoma. After saying goodbye to my wife, I ran through Pioneer Square to King Street Station.

At King Street Station, I boarded the 5:45pm S Line train bound for Lakewood. Unlike Link trains that afternoon , the Sounder train stayed on schedule and we pulled into Tacoma around 6:40pm. I crossed the street to board the T Line, the final Sound Transit service of the day. This left just two more transit modes: Pierce Transit local bus service and the Stream Community Line. Both local buses and the Stream Community Line serve the Pacific Ave corridor, so I exited the T Line train at Convention Center station and walked over to Pacific Ave & S 14th St. A Route 1 bus showed up first so I hopped aboard and rode it two stops to Pacific & 19th. After a few other buses came and went, the last southbound Stream Community Line bus for the day stopped at Pacific & 19th.

I boarded the final bus of the speedrun and took it one stop to Tacoma Dome station. After alighting the bus I stopped the timer to record the first ever ORCA speedrun time: 9 hours, 12 minutes, and 40 seconds.

I really enjoyed spending the day exploring cities across Puget Sound and observing how different transit services are used. The passengers and drivers I spoke with were extremely kind and helpful. I was most surprised by the Kitsap Transit ferries. Every ferry trip I observed was on-time and busy (except for the return trip from Annapolis). Given the geography, the ferries offer a shortcut across the water. These smaller (and cheaper) vessels can provide better service than WSF at a fraction of the cost. More cities and counties should be allowed to operate a fleet of passenger-only ferries. The 35% service reduction in the Seattle – Bremerton Fast Ferry route is incredibly disappointing.

Another highlight of the trip was seeing how an agency’s various transit services benefit the various types of trips. No transit mode is one-size-fits-all so agencies need to adapt the vehicle types (train, bus, boat) to fit their needs. One example of this was in Lynnwood, where Route 166 and the Orange Line cover the same route between Hwy 99 and Lynnwood Transit Center. Despite sharing the same road, the Orange Line only has one stop while Route 166 has four. The Route 166 bus I was on let passengers on/off at three of the four stops. These passengers would have been overlooked with only Orange Line service and Orange Line trips would be much slower with many more stops. The overlapping local and Swift service complement each other nicely. Pierce Transit uses a similar strategy on Pacific Ave with Route 1 and the Stream Community Line.
Here is the complete list of transit services included in the ORCA speedrun:

While most transit agencies in the ORCA pod offer more flexible transit options, the ORCA speedrun only includes fixed route transit. This is primarily to minimize the impact on other transit riders. Flexible services, such as Metro Flex, CT’s Zip Shuttle, or PT’s Runner service, have limited resources. Someone using those services for a speedrun could cause a longer wait for someone else. Fixed route options are acceptable because the impact of one extra rider is negligible.

While planning this adventure I went back and forth on including King County Metro shuttle routes. Metro operates four shuttle routes, but only one (Valley Shuttle) operates year-round. The other three (Waterfront, Golden Gardens, and the snow shuttle) are seasonal or weather dependent. To add another wrinkle, this is an ORCA speedrun and the Waterfront Shuttle is completely free. Ultimately, I decided to make shuttle routes optional.

Also, I chose to separate the T Line from the 1 Line and 2 Line. While they are all technically part of Link, the T Line has little in common with the 1 Line and 2 Line. Another reason to separate the Link lines: Sound Transit reports T Line ridership data to the FTA separate from the 1 Line and 2 Line.
If you plan on attempting this challenge, I hope you can beat my time. Here are a few other rules I followed:

I hope my successful speedrun inspires other Seattle transit enthusiasts to try it as well. While Link receives more of our collective attention than any other mode, trains, buses, and boats throughout Puget Sound play a critical role in getting people where they need to go. Riding each mode is a great way to understand the value it provides to its passengers and to the overall network.

articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.

paras: “Where should I eat in Seattle?” Whether you’re a first-time visitor or a lifer, that question is seemingly simple but the answers are infinitely complex. Some of the main factors to consider are the type of food, price point, neighborhood, and occasion. That’s why Eater’s map of the 38 best restaurants in Seattle exists. This curated list of suggestions attempts to capture the diversity of the food scene in the Seattle metro area, from English pubs serving cumin-y lamb neck meat pies to Indian street food takeout spots, from classic French bistros to modern sushi bars, and so much more.
